title: Dense religious community persists through demographic change while retention, family formation, trust, and political meaning shift
source_unit: Pew Research Center, Tradition and Change Among Latter-day Saints in the U.S., September 22, 2026
geography: United States; adults identifying as Latter-day Saints in the 2023-24 Religious Landscape Study (RLS)

denominator.unit: current Latter-day Saint adults interviewed in the 2023-24 RLS; historical subgroup bases vary

adult_retention.unit: percent of adults raised Latter-day Saint who still identify as Latter-day Saint

adult_retention_2007.unit: percent of adults raised Latter-day Saint who still identified as Latter-day Saint in 2007

religiously_unaffiliated_raised_latter_d.unit: percent of adults raised Latter-day Saint who are now religiously unaffiliated

continuity_change_mechanism.value: High present-day religious commitment can coexist with declining retention and a larger unaffiliated downstream population

observations.method: Pew comparison of the 2023-24 RLS with earlier 2007, 2011, and 2014 Religious Landscape Studies; the 2023-24 RLS interviewed 565 current Latter-day Saints and 316 former members.
observations.uncertainty: Historical comparisons combine older telephone surveys with a 2023-24 study completed mainly online and on paper. Pew reports an experimental telephone comparison supporting the displayed comparisons, but subgroup estimates have margins of error and retention is not a panel observation of the same individuals.
observations.subgroup: Current Latter-day Saints, people raised Latter-day Saint, former members, lifelong members, and converts.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower retention may reflect broader U.S. religious change, cohort replacement, reporting or classification differences, or changes in the meaning of affiliation rather than organizational failure alone.

denominator.unit: current Latter-day Saint adults interviewed in the 2023-24 RLS; subgroup bases vary

white_share.unit: percent of Latter-day Saint adults, down from 85% in 2007

foreign_born_share.unit: percent first generation, compared with 7% in 2007

mountain_region_share.unit: percent of Latter-day Saint adults living in the Census Mountain region

diversification_mechanism.value: A historically concentrated religious identity is becoming more racially and geographically diverse without losing its strong regional core

observations.method: Weighted RLS subgroup estimates compared with Pew’s earlier landscape studies; regional categories follow Census divisions.
observations.uncertainty: Small subgroup bases, rounding, language coverage, and changing survey mode constrain precision. The study notes that Asian estimates represent English speakers and foreign-born estimates represent English- and Spanish-speakers.
observations.subgroup: Race and ethnicity, generation, place of residence, education, and age groups within the Latter-day Saint population.
observations.counterinterpretation: Changing composition may reflect national demographic change and conversion patterns rather than a deliberate organizational transformation; geographic concentration still structures local communal density.

denominator.unit: current Latter-day Saint adults in the RLS; issue-specific subgroup bases vary

lds_republicans_diversity_race.unit: percent of Latter-day Saint Republicans saying a multiracial/multiethnic U.S. strengthens society

all_republicans_diversity_race.unit: percent of all Republicans or Republican leaners

lds_republicans_diversity_religion.unit: percent saying religious diversity strengthens society

all_republicans_diversity_religion.unit: percent of all Republicans or Republican leaners

partisan_cultural_mismatch.value: A strongly Republican religious community can diverge from its partisan peers on immigration and pluralism while remaining more conservative on abortion and homosexuality

observations.method: Pew comparison of Latter-day Saint Republicans or Republican leaners with Republicans nationally in the 2023-24 RLS; reported differences are statistically significant for the displayed issue comparisons.
observations.uncertainty: The survey predates the 2024 presidential election, and partisan identity is not the same as voting, policy action, or institutional influence. Small religious-group bases require attention to confidence intervals.
observations.subgroup: Latter-day Saints, Latter-day Saint Republicans, all Republicans, Mountain-region members, converts, and lifelong members.
observations.counterinterpretation: The pattern may reflect theology, migration and settlement history, education, regional composition, or question wording rather than a stable cross-pressure between religion and party.

observations.period: 2007 to 2023-24; family life, marriage, communal service, and social trust

denominator.unit: current Latter-day Saint adults in the RLS; family and married-item bases vary

recent_volunteering.unit: percent reporting volunteering in the prior 12 months

most_people_trusted.unit: percent saying most people can be trusted

communal_reproduction_mechanism.value: Religious participation supplies family cohesion, volunteering, and generalized trust, but the family form and membership pipeline are changing underneath that communal infrastructure

observations.method: RLS comparisons across religious groups and Latter-day Saint demographic subgroups, with historical comparisons to earlier Pew landscape surveys.
observations.uncertainty: These are self-reports and cross-sectional group comparisons; communal involvement may select for members who remain engaged. Family satisfaction, volunteering, and generalized trust do not establish causal effects of religious membership.
observations.subgroup: Latter-day Saints by education, region, age, marriage, and family status; comparison religious groups and all U.S. adults.
observations.counterinterpretation: High trust and volunteering may reflect selection, local density, education, family resources, or social desirability rather than an institution-specific effect.

related_sources.claim: Pew 2023-24 Religious Landscape Study design and broader religious-group comparison context.
Earlier Pew Latter-day Saint survey used as historical context in the project.

boundary: This record adds a religion-as-social-infrastructure route: communal ties, family practice, volunteering, generalized trust, demographic diversification, retention, and partisan meaning interact without being collapsed into religiosity or electoral behavior. It does not establish causal effects of membership, institutional policy, family wellbeing, political action, or social cohesion.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Pew project landing page plus linked pages on religiousness, political and diversity views, family life, and communal ties reviewed for sample, historical comparisons, subgroup estimates, methodology, and limitations.
reproduction_audit.version_note: Pew’s 2023-24 RLS was conducted mostly before the 2024 presidential election; older surveys used different modes and historical comparisons retain the reported mode-shift caveat.
